tagline.text: Three remote islands off Catanduanes with Bitaog Beach and a lighthouse hill

location.label: Location
location.text: Northwest sea off Caramoran, Catanduanes (Maqueda Channel)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: February–May, when the sea is calm

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,000~6,000 (boat, meals and camping from Caramoran; Manila round-trip transport not included)

children.text: The Palumbanes Islands are three islands off Caramoran on Catanduanes: Parongpong, Tignob and Calabagio. A boat ride of 30 minutes to 1 hour gets you there, and you will find white-sand Bitaog Beach, windswept hills and coral snorkeling, but almost no facilities on these remote islands.

The Palumbanes Islands (locally called Parompong) are a small cluster of islands in the northwest of Catanduanes province in the Bicol Region, just off the town of Caramoran. The three main islands are Parongpong, the largest, Tignob and Calabagio, and they belong administratively to Caramoran. Seen from the main island of Catanduanes, they lie a little over
13km
away, so with good weather they are not hard to reach by boat. The islands face the Philippine Sea, so they take the full force of wind and waves.

What people love about these islands is the quiet, which is nothing like a typical tourist spot. You will find cream-to-white sand, clear blue water, hills where the grass ripples like a sea, and a simple fishing village life that has stayed as it was. Local guides even call the area the fishing paradise of the north. In exchange, there are almost no resorts or restaurants, so think of it as a place you prepare for rather than a place you simply go to relax.

The best-known spot on the islands is Bitaog Beach on Parongpong Island. It is the place most often recommended for camping and photos, and on windy days the waves can be good enough for surfing or skimboarding. Tignob Island is visible in front of the beach, and you can cross to it on an island-hopping trip to see shallow coral and tropical fish. A lighthouse stands on the hill at the top of the island and is a popular sunset walk.
Getting here takes effort: Catanduanes is far from Manila, and Caramoran is at the northern end, about
86km

from the provincial capital Virac. For that reason, most visitors set aside a day or a night for the Palumbanes in the middle of a Catanduanes tour. There are few facilities, but there are also few people, which suits travelers who like quiet islands. Caramoran is a quiet coastal town of about 30,000 people according to the 2024 census, with heavy rainfall of roughly 3,200–4,200 mm a year (4,190 mm in the Wikipedia climate table, 3,188 mm in PAGASA's normals for Virac on the south of the island; sources differ) and an average daily high of around
. Check the sky and sea first when planning, and allow for the chance that your boat cannot sail on the day you booked.

This is the most famous beach on Parongpong Island, with cream-to-white sand and clear water. It is most often picked for camping and photos, and it is said that no entrance fee is charged. When the wind picks up, the waves can be good enough for surfing.
Travelers report good coral about

out from the far left side of the beach as your boat approaches. There is nowhere on the island to rent gear, so be sure to bring your own mask and snorkel. Keep your fins raised while swimming so you do not step on or touch the coral.
This small island lies directly in front of Bitaog Beach, and you reach it on an island-hopping trip. Visitors report plate corals in
of water off the south beach. Diving and snorkeling spots are said to be nearby.
This small island is a stop on the way back to the main island, and corals are also said to grow here. Tell your boatman in advance that you want it included in your island-hopping route.

The lighthouse hill at the top of the island is a place for a sunset walk and views. The trail is steep and rocky, and many visitors recommend going with a local guide. Sturdy shoes are safer than flip-flops.

This is described as a trekking spot where tall grass ripples like the sea when the wind blows early in the morning. The 360-degree views, rock formations and grassland make it a good place for photos.
This shallow beach on the north of the island has a rocky islet and waves coming from far away. Sea urchins are reported on the way there, so wear shoes when you walk.

In the island village you can look around the market and try local home cooking. The basics are simple: rice with jackfruit (langka) and fish cooked in coconut milk. Many local people make their living by fishing, and watching the boats come back early in the morning and the fish being traded is a good experience.
Find a boat at the port of Baybay village in Caramoran, agree on the fare in advance and check the life jackets.
The boat ride to Parongpong Island takes about
30 minutes–1 hour
, depending on weather and waves.
Swim and snorkel at Bitaog Beach, then tour Tignob Island and Calabagio Island by boat.
Have lunch on the beach. There are almost no restaurants on the island, so bring a packed lunch and water.
Head back to Caramoran, watching the wind and weather. It is safer to leave before the waves rise.
You can add a trip along the road toward Pandan to Tuwad Tuwadan Lagoon or the Cagnipa Rolling Hills.
A local tour operator's day tour combined with Pandan is listed as hotel pickup at 5:00, departure from Caramoran at 7:00, lunch at Bitaog at 12:00 and return at 13:00.
Take a boat from Caramoran and pitch your tent near Bitaog Beach. It is good manners to ask permission from the village first.
Spend your time snorkeling and walking along the beach.
Climb the lighthouse hill to watch the sunset. The way back is dark, so bring a flashlight.
Early in the windy morning, see the grassland scenery from Binanderahan Hill.
Pack up all your trash and take the boat back.
Electricity runs for only a few hours a day, so the nights are very dark and quiet. On a clear night the stars are great.
There are direct flights from Manila to Virac Airport (VRC), the provincial capital of Catanduanes, but they do not run often, so check the airline schedule before you go.
From Virac to Baybay village in Caramoran, take a bus or van toward Pandan and travel about
86km
. One review says it takes about 5 hours, so confirm the time locally.

We could not confirm any regular passenger ferry. You have to find a boatman locally.
Local guides say the sea is calm in the dry season from February to May. This is the safest time and visibility is good.

Caramoran has a climate with heavy rainfall all year. In PAGASA's 1991–2020 normals for Virac, February to May get only about 140–180 mm a month, while October to December get about 400–520 mm. Reviews say the weather is rough from October to early January. Boats may be unable to sail then, so check the latest weather and your boatman's judgment.

The sea is calm from February to May, but the midday sun is very strong. There is little shade on the islands, so bring a hat, sunscreen and a long-sleeved rash guard. In the rainy season, on the other hand, boats rock and the water can turn cloudy, which lowers snorkeling visibility.

There is almost no formal accommodation on the islands. A few unmaintained huts are said to exist, but their condition is not guaranteed, so many guides tell you to bring a tent. If you want to stay in the village, ask the local school or villagers first, and it is polite to leave a small gift of money when you go.

It is more practical to eat and sleep on the Caramoran side. Baybay village has cheap carinderias (local eateries), and shops on the island bring goods from the mainland, so prices are higher. Prepare water, snacks and medicine in Caramoran or Virac. Virac has accommodation in town.

Food centers on rice and fish. Island families often eat fish cooked in coconut milk with jackfruit, and Caramoran on the mainland has inexpensive local eateries. If you camp, bring a stove, a cooking pot and ready-to-eat food from the mainland. Island shops sell only the basics at higher prices than the mainland. The easiest routine is to shop in the morning and load everything straight onto the boat.
Bring your own mask, snorkel and life jacket. It is hard to rent gear on the island.
Drinking water is very scarce. Bring plenty of water to drink.
Electricity runs only a few hours a day (around 5 p.m. to 10 p.m.). Bring a power bank.
The boat ride is rough and you get wet easily, so a waterproof bag and zip bags help.
Bring enough cash and small bills. Expect to find almost nowhere on the island that takes cards, so withdraw money on the mainland beforehand.
Do not step on coral, and ask the boatman not to let the boat touch the coral.
Take all your trash with you. The only rule in local guidance is to leave no trash behind.
The lighthouse hill trail is rough, so wear sturdy shoes.
If you are touring Catanduanes, plan the Palumbanes as the northwest end of your route and check the boat schedule between Virac and Tabaco in advance.
Agree with your boatman before you leave on the island-hopping order (Bitaog, Tignob, Calabagio) and the time you will come back.
These are remote islands with no regular passenger ferry and almost no accommodation. In bad weather the boat may not sail, and your return can be delayed.
From October to January the waves are high and sailing is difficult. Check the weather on the morning of your trip and your boatman's judgment.
Bring plenty of personal medicine.
Sea urchins are reported on the way to Cuyabot Beach.
Some of the cost and boat fare information relies on older reviews, so check it again locally.
Do not get on a boat without a life jacket.
Medicine is said to be hard to find on the islands. In an emergency you may have to come back to the mainland by boat, so arrange insurance and emergency contacts in advance.
The island that holds the Palumbanes, with the road from Virac to Caramoran running overland.
A highlight on the east coast of Catanduanes, which you can add to a tour of the main island.
Caramoran is described as having the white beaches of Toytoy and Sabang and the Ab-haw, Awinis and Garagag waterfalls. If the islands are not possible, they make a good alternative on the mainland.
In tour operators' itineraries, island hopping is followed by Pandan's Tuwad Tuwadan Lagoon and the Cagnipa Rolling Hills.
